title: Explaining Hall-effect, TMR, and other new types of "mechanical" switches
gist: A consumer guide to contactless keyboard switches (optical, capacitive, Hall-effect, TMR, inductive) arguing the gaming-latency and longevity advantages are real but mostly imperceptible to average users, while premium pricing and fragmented, hard-to-source components limit the ecosystem. The newest sensing tech (TMR, inductive) trades on power efficiency and noise immunity but remains scarce and costlier.

insights.claim: Contactless keyboards (optical, Hall-effect and others) have grown common over six years and often sell at higher prices than traditional mechanical boards, in return for theoretical gaming advantages that are subtle in daily use.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Premiumization of a niche peripheral category rests on benefits most buyers cannot perceive.
insights.locator: The mechanical keyboard isn't always so mechanical

insights.claim: Optical switches are technically faster because they need no debouncing, but an average person typing an email would almost certainly not notice the quicker input.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Latency marketing targets a tiny pro-gamer segment; mass-market upgrade demand is limited.

insights.claim: Total keyboard latency depends on travel, actuation time and polling rate, not just sensing tech: a Bluetooth full-height optical board at 133 Hz polling will lag a wired low-profile mechanical board at 8,000 Hz.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Sensing technology is a minor lever in the latency chain; spec-sheet comparisons mislead.
insights.locator: But keyboard latency, or the amount of time

insights.claim: Only professional gamers need ultra-low-latency keyboards, and even they are assumed to have already optimized GPU, CPU and monitor first.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Addressable market for latency-driven switch premiums is narrow.
insights.locator: Again, for many of us, none of this matters

insights.claim: Vendors tailor contactless switches to gamers, so linear options far outnumber tactile or clicky ones.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Gaming demand shapes product mix, leaving typists underserved.
insights.locator: And because contactless switches frequently target gamers

insights.claim: Debounce delays are commonly cited by enthusiasts at 5 ms to 20 ms, manufacturers rarely disclose them, and some makers use longer-than-necessary debounce to compensate for switch degradation; Cherry says some MX2A switches need under 1 ms.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Modern mechanical switches are closing the latency gap, eroding the contactless pitch.
insights.locator: Most of us never notice debounce delays

insights.claim: A Razer marketing image claiming optical switches respond faster than magnetic and mechanical ones should be taken with a grain of salt.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Vendor-supplied response-time comparisons are unreliable evidence.

insights.claim: Contactless switches avoid oxidation and corrosion of metal leaves, but newer mechanical switches such as some Cherry MX2A rated for 100 million keystrokes can match their lifespans.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: The durability premium is shrinking as incumbents upgrade.

insights.claim: Feel depends more on specs, force curve and materials than on whether a switch is mechanical, optical or magnetic; lubricated premium mechanical switches can feel extremely smooth.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Sensing tech is not a differentiator for typing feel.
insights.locator: If you want the best-feeling switches

insights.claim: Contactless switches need specialized PCBs, and hot-swappable PCBs and prebuilt hot-swap keyboards for them are harder to find, which undercuts the repairability and longevity argument.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Ecosystem fragmentation raises switching costs and lock-in.

insights.claim: Razer's optical keyboards are built as fixed assemblies for precise alignment rather than hot-swappable, and Razer's longevity-based justification does not address customizability.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Vendors favor sealed designs that limit aftermarket modularity.

insights.claim: Contactless switches enable adjustable actuation points, dual-input per press and analog input, features impossible on traditional mechanical switches and the real functional differentiator for gamers.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Software-defined input is the durable value layer, favoring firmware-strong vendors.

insights.claim: RTINGs tested 14 keyboards from 11 brands with adjustable actuation and found every one actuated at a different distance than set in the companion app, by fractions of a millimeter.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Advertised precision outruns real calibration across the industry.

insights.claim: Hall-effect keyboards reached prebuilt gaming products in 2021 starting with Wooting's Two HE, and TMR keyboards became available in 2024.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Sensor technology cycles are now roughly three years apart.

insights.claim: TMR sensors generally use less power and offer a better signal-to-noise ratio than Hall-effect sensors, which often need signal amplification, so TMR boards can have longer battery life and less noise susceptibility.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: TMR advantage is efficiency and noise immunity, relevant to wireless products.

insights.claim: TMR's higher peak sensitivity can allow actuation points in 0.01 mm increments versus the common 0.1 mm, but some Hall-effect keyboards beat some TMR keyboards because sensor placement, polling rate and firmware also matter.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Implementation quality, not sensor class alone, drives performance.

insights.claim: TMR keyboards cost more than similarly specced Hall-effect boards due to higher wafer and packaging costs and shorter time in market, and TMR switches, PCBs and kits are hard to find.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: TMR remains supply-constrained and premium; scale could compress costs.

insights.claim: Keychron labeled its TMR keyboards 'HE' because Hall-effect was the widely known magnetic term, so some TMR boards are marketed as Hall-effect despite TMR's benefits.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Consumer awareness of TMR is low; branding lags technology.
insights.locator: Some companies have marketed TMR keyboards

insights.claim: Magnetic switches are fragmented: 3-pin versus 5-pin, magnet polarity and flux ranges (e.g. 120-750 Gs versus 102-905 Gs) can make switches incompatible with another PCB, and there is no standard for measuring magnetic flux.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Lack of standards limits aftermarket interchangeability and favors vertically integrated vendors.

insights.claim: Keychron says magnetic flux is an internal engineering parameter and uses firmware calibration per switch, while Monsgeek publishes flux specs for enthusiasts, showing divergent vendor transparency.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Calibration-in-firmware is a vendor moat.
insights.locator: Keychron doesn't provide magnetic flux specs

insights.claim: Magnetic keyboards can occasionally act erratically near other electronics due to electromagnetic noise or external fields, and hot-swap mechanical sockets are hard to implement because the sensor must stay aligned with the magnet.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Design constraints limit modularity of magnetic boards.

insights.claim: Inductive-switch keyboards first reached consumers last year, can use less power than Hall-effect and TMR boards because they need no per-key sensor, and resist magnetic interference because switches contain no magnets.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Inductive is the emerging low-power, interference-free alternative to magnetic sensing.

insights.claim: Cherry's precision claims for inductive switches are unproven; RTINGs found the One X's accuracy impressive but not better than the best Hall-effect keyboards.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Inductive is not yet shown to beat entrenched Hall-effect on accuracy.

insights.claim: Only Cherry, Kailh and Unionwell appear to make inductive switches, with Aesco partnering with Unionwell and Kailh, and only Kailh seems to sell switches individually, so most inductive switches ship only in prebuilt keyboards.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: A concentrated supply base gives component makers leverage in this nascent category.

insights.claim: Topre capacitive keyboards remain among the most expensive, with HHKB's Professional Classic Type-S at $269 even without arrows or numpad.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: A durable premium niche exists for feel-led keyboards independent of gaming.
